title: Stratified Probing and Slotting Journal
body:
Purpose
This is a living experiment journal for a different angle on continuous-batching tuning: rather than only tuning timeouts and global batch limits, we introduced stratified probing and slotting to reduce tail latency while improving fairness for mixed-priority workloads. The idea: partition incoming requests into age-based and priority-based "slots" that get periodically probed/coalesced into batches with adaptive thresholds.

Background / Motivation
- Existing adaptive batchers were reducing mean cost but exposing multi-modal tail behavior under mixed short/long sequence mixes and bursty arrivals.
- Observed symptoms: p99.9 spikes when a handful of long-seq requests occupy GPU slots while many short jobs wait; also starvation when aggressive coalescing waits for size without respecting age/fairness.
- Hypothesis: if we proactively stratify the queue and use targeted probes to form minimal-effort batches for older/short-priority slots, we can reduce extreme tails without raising overall cost materially.

High-level approach
1) Stratified slotting: requests are assigned to one of three slot buckets at enqueue time: fast (short expected tokens/low compute), standard (default), and long (large sequences or heavy-kv usage). Assignment uses route hints + inference of length from prompt tokens.
2) Age bands: within each slot, track arrival age bands (0-10ms, 10-50ms, 50-200ms, 200ms+). 
3) Probing: every probe_tick (initially 10ms) we sample head-of-queue from each band with a probability that scales with age band. A successful probe can trigger a small batch flush for that slot without waiting for global size.
4) Slot quotas & slot-stealing: to prevent long-slot dominance, have per-GPU slot quotas (e.g., 40% fast, 40% standard, 20% long) with ephemeral slot-stealing when there is unused capacity.
5) Fairness decay: track served_count per client-id and apply soft demotion to clients exceeding per-window budget (helps noisy neighbors).

Experiment matrix (configs tried)
- Probe tick: 5ms / 10ms / 25ms
- Probe sample weight per age band: linear vs exponential (older ages get higher prob)
- Per-GPU quotas: 30/50/20 vs 40/40/20 vs 50/30/20
- Small-batch max size on probe-trigger: 4 / 8 / 16
- Slot steal threshold: idle_time 100ms / 250ms

Workloads
- Synthetic blended trace composed from: 60% short (mean 8 tokens, std 3), 30% standard (mean 64 tokens), 10% long (mean 512 tokens). Poisson arrival rate scaled to achieve GPU occupancy ~85%.
- Real traffic sample from route /chat/early-adopter daytime window (anonymized).

Instrumentation and profiling
- Added additional tracing spans at enqueue -> probe -> batch-formation -> kernel-launch. Each span emits GPU-local queue depth and KV cache hit indicator.
- Enabled lightweight eBPF-based syscall traces on hosts to correlate kernel stalls with probe timings.
- CUDA kernel timing via CUPTI hooks aggregated per model-shard; also captured GPU SM utilization and memory bandwidth (nvprof lighter summary).
- CPU flamegraphs (perf + async-profiler) for the path that assembles batches from multiple slots.

Key findings (summary)
- p99 reduced by 38% in best configs vs baseline adaptive coalescer (no slotting) on synthetic blended trace. p99.9 improved by ~50% for short-priority requests.
- Cost (token-GPU-sec) increased by ~2.5% in the best slotting config; tradeoff looks acceptable.
- Probe tick too frequent (5ms) caused CPU overhead and slightly increased jitter; 10ms was best balance. 25ms missed opportunity for older requests, increasing p99 tail again.
- Quotas matter: 50/30/20 favored short request latency but starved long-job throughput, causing queueing on long slot and occasional timeouts. 40/40/20 was best balanced.
- Slot-stealing with idle_time 100ms introduced occasional preemption cost (context switching overhead) on GPU memory footprint when stolen slots had large KV caches; 250ms safer but slightly higher tail.
- Fairness decay prevented a small set of high-throughput clients from monopolizing probe-triggered small batches; without it, p95 for other clients drifted upward over sustained periods.

Representative numbers (synthetic blended trace, GPU pool of 8 A100-s with quantized model):
- Baseline: p50=12ms, p95=45ms, p99=210ms, p99.9=420ms, mean-cost=1.00x
- Stratified (probe 10ms, quotas 40/40/20, small-batch=8): p50=11ms, p95=38ms, p99=130ms, p99.9=210ms, mean-cost=1.025x

Deeper profiling observations
- Many p99 events in baseline were due to head-of-queue long jobs forming giant batches to amortize kernel startup: this delayed short jobs behind them. With slotting, probes flush shorter buckets and avoid clumping.
- GPU SM utilization saw more consistent ramp with slotting; baseline had sawtooth patterns where one batch would run long and leave cores underutilized for small requests waiting.
- KV cache hit-rate for short requests improved slightly (3%) because short-slot probe flushes reused recently warmed KV state.
- CPU overhead from probing logic is small (<3% CPU on batch builder thread) at 10ms tick; at 5ms it grew to ~9% and affected latency jitter.

Failure modes and caveats
- If route hints are noisy/misclassified, long requests can end up in fast slot and then be demoted only after consuming probe time; mitigations: conservative assignment + early detection by sequence length after tokenization.
- Memory pressure when slot-stealing a long slot can cause eviction and slowdowns; we need GPU memory-aware slot-stealing heuristics.
- Workloads with uniformly long sequences see no win; slotting overhead then is pure cost. Detect and turn slotting off for such routes automatically.

Next steps and action items
- Add model-led assignment: use ML model to predict cost bucket at enqueue based on prompt features (Priya lead).
- Implement GPU-memory-aware slot stealing and probe backoff when memory fragmentation detected (Mateo lead).
- Add automatic route classifier to turn slotting on/off per-route (Liang lead).
- Run a 48h canary against production synthetic load with safety limits (SLO: no >2x p99 increase for any route).
- PR followup: performance tests in CI replicating probe tick variations (github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1284).

Appendix: quick config snippets tested
- config A: {probe_tick_ms=10, age_weights=[1,2,5,10], quotas=[40,40,20], small_batch_max=8, slot_steal_idle_ms=250}
- config B: {probe_tick_ms=5, age_weights=[1,3,9,27], quotas=[50,30,20], small_batch_max=4, slot_steal_idle_ms=100}
- config C: {probe_tick_ms=25, age_weights=[1,1,2,4], quotas=[30,50,20], small_batch_max=16, slot_steal_idle_ms=250}

Notes to reviewers
- This journal contains a mix of raw observations and early interpretations. Please comment inline if you see measurement bias or if you can reproduce on different hardware. Main objective: converge on a safe default slotting config that reduces extreme tails for multi-modal traffic without causing regressions for homogeneous or long-only workloads.

- Wire in dashboard for slot-level metrics (served_count, avg_age, avg_batch_size) (Priya)
- Add gating flag to console for turning slotting on per deployment (SRE consult)

End of journal entry.
